title: Port scanning with nmap
summary: Map which hosts exist and what they expose, the way attackers and defenders both do.

steps.title: How a scan works
body: > Only scan networks you own or have written permission to test. Scanning other people's systems can be illegal.
nmap uses the TCP handshake. To test a port it sends a SYN and reads the reply:
| RST | host is up, nothing listening | `closed` |
Host discovery (`-sn`) skips ports and just checks which addresses answer. On a local network it uses ARP, which is fast and hard to block.

steps.prompt: Match each reply to nmap's verdict.

steps.title: Commands
body: nmap -p 80 --open 10.15.1.0/24     # one port across a range, show only open
nc 10.15.1.20 21                   # talk to a service by hand

steps.prompt: Complete the command: scan **all** ports on 10.15.1.20 with faster timing, then identify versions on 21 and 80.
Match each port to its service.
An admin moved SSH to port 47022 "so nobody finds it". A default `nmap 10.15.1.20` doesn't show it. What's the honest assessment?
options: `nmap -p-` finds it in seconds; obscurity reduces log noise but is not a control
It's safe as long as the banner is removed
steps.explain: Default scans check the top 1,000 ports. Real attackers scan them all.

steps.prompt: nmap reports this for a host. Exactly how many ports are `open`? Type the number.
steps.explain: `closed` (RST) and `filtered` (no answer) aren't open. `filtered` on 5432 means a firewall is doing its job.

lines: Scan all ports on each host with `-p-`
Compare against what should be exposed and close the rest

steps.title: Write the scan report
prompt: Write `List<string> Report(Dictionary<int, string> replies)` where each value is the reply seen for that port: `"syn-ack"`, `"rst"` or `"none"`.
Return lines for **open ports only**, sorted by port, formatted like nmap: `"{port}/tcp open {service}"`, where the service is from this table, else `unknown`:
21 ftp, 22 ssh, 25 smtp, 53 domain, 80 http, 443 https, 445 microsoft-ds, 3306 mysql, 3389 ms-wbt-server, 5432 postgresql.
template: Dojo.Eq("open only, sorted", new List<string> { "21/tcp open ftp", "80/tcp open http", "47022/tcp open unknown" }, Report(dojoR));
Dojo.Eq("nothing open", new List<string>(), Report(new Dictionary<int, string> { [22] = "none" }));

steps.title: Compare with the inventory
prompt: Write `(List<int> Unexpected, List<int> Missing) Drift(List<int> openPorts, List<int> expected)`:
ports open but not expected (a finding), and expected but not open (a broken service). Both sorted ascending, no duplicates.
starter: (List<int> Unexpected, List<int> Missing) Drift(List<int> openPorts, List<int> expected)
solution: (List<int> Unexpected, List<int> Missing) Drift(List<int> openPorts, List<int> expected)
template: var dojoD = Drift(new List<int> { 443, 21, 22, 21 }, new List<int> { 22, 443, 80 });
hints: `Except` gives the set difference without duplicates.
